paragraphs.text: A loose [oolong](oolong:definition) from Guangdong, made in the 1980s. The trade knows the province for one oolong above all, the [dancong](guangdong:phoenix-dancong) of Phoenix Mountain in Chaozhou. A label that names only Guangdong, though, does not say which mountain or village a tea comes from.

At forty-one years, this is oolong that was kept rather than drunk fresh. Only well-made oolong is put aside like this, because [roasting](oolong:oxidation-and-roast) lowers the moisture so the leaf keeps. Damp is the danger over the years. Oolong held this long is usually [roasted again at low heat](oolong:ageing) from time to time to drive off what it has taken in, a skilled job that can cost some quality each round. The trade has no agreed age at which an oolong counts as aged.

brewing.text: Oolong is most often brewed gongfu style, in a small gaiwan or clay pot with plenty of leaf and short steeps, and it stands many rounds. A common start is about 4 to 6 grams to 100 ml, with a first steep of roughly 5 to 15 seconds and 5 to 10 seconds more each round. Light, green-style oolong takes water a little off the boil, about 90 to 95°C; heavily oxidised, roasted and aged oolong takes water at a full boil. Many people pour a quick first rinse to wake tightly rolled leaf. In a larger pot, use less leaf and steep for a few minutes.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow and sweet cup, often with dried fruit or plum and wood, sometimes something herbal, little astringency, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
